reading.body:
Banking is where AI governance predates the AI boom by more than a decade: Fed SR 11-7 model risk rules already cover credit and AML models, and generative AI in service and compliance is the new supervised frontier.

The pattern is that banking's AI oversight is older than the current generative wave. Credit and AML models have operated under SR 11-7 since 2011, so the sector enters the generative era with pre-existing validation, documentation, and model risk requirements. Treasury's report frames the supervisory conversation, and the Evident AI Banking Index provides a public scoreboard across talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency.

For AI specifically, this means generative deployments in service and compliance inherit a governance burden that most other industries lack. A bank cannot launch a customer-facing chatbot or compliance assistant without treating it as a model under SR 11-7, which slows deployment but also reduces the chance of unmanaged failures. The data does not show scale. It contains no figures on compute demand or power consumption for banking AI, and no adoption rates or model sizes. Governance is the constraint the data documents, not infrastructure.

summary: Fraud detection and credit modelling are decades old; generative AI in service and compliance is the new supervised frontier.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use in finance and insurance, NAICS 52, at 41.0% in the latest reading, up from 36.5% in the prior period. The question asked is whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, and the first time it was asked was September 2023. That makes banking and insurance one of the more measured adopters in the survey rather than a speculative one, and the direction of travel between the two periods is upward.

What the curated material emphasizes is that this sector did not arrive at AI recently. According to this site's own coverage, credit and anti-money-laundering models have operated for years under the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 model risk management guidance, issued in 2011, which the Fed lists in its 2011 supervisory letters index. The practical consequence is that banking is the sector where AI governance predates the current AI boom by more than a decade. A bank deploying a generative model today is not writing on a blank page, it is fitting a new tool into an existing supervisory frame that already expects documentation, validation, and ongoing monitoring of models.

The sources also point to where the public conversation is being shaped. Treasury's report on AI in financial services, covering uses, opportunities, and risks, is described here as framing the US supervisory conversation, which places the policy agenda with the Treasury rather than with any single agency. On the private side, the Evident AI Banking Index is described as the benchmark, scoring the major global banks across dozens of quantitative maturity metrics including talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency, and as the closest thing banking has to a public AI scoreboard. This site's Financial Models section tracks models tuned for financial text, drawn from the Hugging Face Hub public API and sorted by all-time downloads, with tag provenance stated.

The material is thinner on deployment specifics than a reader might want. The excerpts do not report which banks run which systems, what share of fraud detection or compliance work is automated, or what returns institutions are seeing. The one concrete regulatory artifact in the excerpts, the Federal Reserve letter, is a 2011 guidance regarding prior notices with respect to dividend declarations by savings association subsidiaries of savings and loan holding companies, which is cited here for the existence of the SR 11-7 regime rather than for its own contents. The Treasury excerpt in the JSON is a sanctions press release about a gold smuggling and money laundering network, not the AI report itself, so the risk framing attributed to Treasury comes from this site's summary rather than from the harvested text.

For someone deciding whether to deploy, the picture the sources support is one of a sector with a high measured adoption rate, an established supervisory expectation that models be governed, and a public benchmarking culture that makes maturity comparisons possible. The gaps are equally instructive. The sources do not supply ROI figures for banking AI, do not name vendors, and do not quantify where spending concentrates, so any claim about returns or market share would go beyond what is here. What can be said is that the compliance and model risk function is not an afterthought in this sector, it is the inherited operating environment, and the Federal Reserve's guidance and Treasury's framing are the two poles a deployment decision has to answer to.

https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-rel.brief: On International Anti-Corruption Day, Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned 28 individuals and businesses tied to a Zimbabwe-based gold smuggling and money-laundering network led by Kamlesh Pattni. The Treasury says the scheme bribed officials, used trusted supporters to conceal ownership, and built a global web of companies to hide illicit activity, depriving Zimbabwe’s citizens of resource benefits while enriching corrupt officials and criminals. Acting Under Secretary Bradley T. Smith noted that “Corruption respects no borders” and that the action demonstrates a whole-of-government approach and collaboration with allies. The Treasury’s move is carried out under Executive Order 13818, which targets serious human-rights abuse and corruption worldwide. International Anti-Corruption Day, observed annually on December 9 since the 2003 UNCAC, aims to raise awareness of anti-corruption initiatives; the United Nations lists 189 parties to the convention.

https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisi.brief: This page lists the Federal Reserve Board of Governors’ 2011 supervision and regulation letters. It notes that a lock icon or https indicates a secure .gov connection and advises “Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.” It also contains guidance on prior notices concerning dividend declarations by savings association subsidiaries of savings and loan holding companies.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The page catalogues the 1000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub, listing each model's licence, download count and release date, and states that the list is refreshed daily. It says the data comes from the Hugging Face Hub public API, sorted by all-time downloads, with every model linking to its own Hub page. The page reports that it was last verified on 2026-10-06 and gives a citation format crediting The World of AI. It also notes that searches cover the full text of every published page on the site, which it says is rebuilt daily from primary sources.
